prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The five views place a large table directly in front of the camera wearer at roughly 0.3–1.2 m, with the tablet/paper at the near edge about 0.3–0.5 m away, laptops across the table about 0.7–1.1 m away, and seated people beyond them roughly 1–2 m away. Brighter regions clarify that the camera wearer’s hands and tablet are nearest, the tabletop and laptops are intermediate, and people, chairs, walls, and cabinets are farther away; nearby people and objects across the table are generally separated by about 0.3–1 m. Across frames, the tablet rises and shifts toward the centre, while the view rotates right until a person and an extended arm enter prominently from the right in frame 5, making that hand one of the nearest visible regions. The map also exposes depth ordering where RGB textures overlap, including hands in front of the tablet, laptops in front of people, and people in front of the rear wall, but it is unreliable at thin hands, object boundaries, black missing regions, and metrically precise distance because the grayscale depth is smooth and uncalibrated.
descriptions.segmentation: The masks identify several people around a dining table, multiple laptops on the tabletop, chairs behind them, and a book or paper-like object near the centre, making overlapping object extents clearer than in RGB. People appear partly cut off along the left, upper, and right borders, while laptops overlap the table and occlude parts of the seated people; the masks show which visible fragments belong to people versus furniture even when RGB colours are similar. From left to right in time, the camera turns right: left-side people and objects move out of view, the central laptop/table regions shift left, and a right-side person becomes large and partially cropped in frame 5, roughly 0.5–1.5 m from the wearer, with other people about 1–2 m away across the table. The map supports left/right and overlap relationships but gives no direct metric depth or reliable facing direction, and several masks change colour or shape between frames, merge with neighbouring regions, omit thin limbs, or assign implausible classes and boundaries.
descriptions.pose: The skeleton map is mostly empty: it detects a small magenta hand configuration near the centre in frame 3, then in frame 5 detects magenta hands and a yellow upper-body skeleton near the upper-right. In frame 5, the yellow figure is to the right and farther than the clustered magenta hands, with head and shoulders above the hands; the body orientation appears oblique rather than fully frontal, but the sparse face landmarks do not reliably establish eye contact with the camera wearer. The hand detections show articulated finger locations and overlapping hands that are difficult to separate in RGB, placing them approximately within 0.3–0.8 m of the wearer and near the right-side person’s arm’s reach, while the detected torso is roughly 1–2 m away. The absence of skeletons in most frames is unreliable rather than evidence that no people are present, because the RGB and segmentation maps show several seated people whose bodies are cropped, occluded by the table and laptops, or too incomplete for pose detection.
